question: How long is the liquid amoxicillin from the pharmacy good for, and does it need to go in the fridge?
reference_answer: The mixed liquid amoxicillin must be kept refrigerated and thrown out after 14 days.

Common Side Effects
• Diarrhea (most common, due to disruption of normal gut bacteria)
• Nausea, vomiting, or stomach pain
• Diaper rash or yeast infection (thrush) due to disruption of normal flora
• Skin rash (non-allergic amoxicillin rash is common, especially with viral infections)
• Contact the doctor if side effects are severe or if a rash with hives or swelling develops
Probiotics During Antibiotic Use
Some pediatricians recommend giving a probiotic (such as Culturelle Kids or Florastor Kids) during and for a

answer: Reconstituted liquid amoxicillin must be refrigerated and should be discarded after 14 days [S1].

question: The school nurse found lice on my kid. Does she have to be sent home right away?
reference_answer: No. The AAP and CDC don't recommend no-nit policies; a child with lice can finish the school day, start treatment that evening, and return after the first treatment.
source_excerpts:
[pediatric-medical-reference.pdf#26]
Common Myths
• Myth: Lice can jump or fly. Fact: lice can only crawl. They spread through direct head-to-head contact
• Myth: Lice prefer dirty hair. Fact: lice actually prefer clean hair because it is easier to attach to
• Myth: You need to deep clean the whole house. Fact: lice die within 1 to 2 days without a human host. Focus on items that contacted the head in the past 48 hours
• Myth: Nits on hair shafts far from the scalp are a current infestation. Fact: nits more than a quarter inch
from the scalp are likely already hatched or dead
School Policies
The AAP and CDC do not recommend no-nit policies (keeping children out of school until all nits are removed). Children with active lice can finish the school day and start treatment at home that evening. They can return to
school after the first treatment. The goal is to minimize disruption to the child's education while managing the
infestation effectively. Source: MedlinePlus/NIH, CDC Head Lice Information, AAP Head Lice Guidelines
answer: No, your child does not have to be sent home right away. Children with active lice can finish the school day and start treatment at home that evening. They can return to school after the first treatment [S1].

question: My son has croup with a barking cough. What signs mean I should call 911 right away?
reference_answer: Call 911 if the child has blue or gray lips or fingertips, is struggling to breathe, cannot speak or cry because of breathing difficulty, or is drooling and unable to swallow.
source_excerpts:
[pediatric-medical-reference.pdf#5]
3. Croup
What Is Croup
Croup is a common childhood illness that causes swelling of the voice box (larynx), windpipe (trachea), and
bronchial tubes (bronchi). It causes a distinctive barking cough that sounds like a seal. Croup is most common
in children aged 6 months to 3 years, with peak incidence around age 2. It most often occurs in fall and winter. Croup is usually caused by a viral infection, most commonly parainfluenza virus. Other viruses including RSV,
influenza, and adenovirus can also cause croup. Symptoms
• A harsh, barking cough (the hallmark symptom, often described as sounding like a seal)
• Stridor: a high-pitched, squeaky, or whistling sound when breathing in (inspiratory stridor)
• Hoarse or raspy voice
• Fever, usually low-grade but can be higher
• Runny nose and cold-like symptoms (often precede the cough by 1 to 2 days)
• Symptoms typically worsen at night and with crying or agitation
• Symptoms usually peak on the second or third night and resolve within a week
Severity Levels
Mild croup: occasional barking cough, no stridor at rest, no significant breathing difficulty. Moderate croup:
frequent barking cough, stridor at rest, mild chest retractions (skin pulling in between ribs or at the neck). Severe croup: significant stridor at rest, marked retractions, agitation, decreased air entry, possible cyanosis
(blue coloring). Severe croup requires emergency care. Treatment and Home Care
• Keep the child calm and comfortable. Crying and agitation worsen symptoms significantly
• Cool mist: take the child outside into cool night air for 10 to 15 minutes, or sit in a bathroom with cool mist
from the shower. Cool moist air can help reduce airway swelling
• Steam: sit in a closed bathroom with a hot shower running to create steam. This can help some children,
though evidence is mixed
• Keep the child upright or propped up to ease breathing
• Offer warm clear fluids to soothe the throat and keep the child hydrated
• Acetaminophen or ibuprofen for fever and discomfort
• For moderate to severe croup, a doctor may prescribe oral dexamethasone (a steroid) to reduce airway
swelling. A single dose often provides dramatic improvement
• In emergency settings, nebulized epinephrine may be given for severe symptoms. This provides rapid but
temporary relief
When to Go to the ER
Call 911 immediately if the child has blue or gray lips or fingertips, is struggling to breathe, cannot speak or
I
cry due to breathing difficulty, or is drooling and unable to swallow
• Stridor that is getting louder or does not stop at rest
answer: Call 911 immediately if your child has blue or gray lips or fingertips, is struggling to breathe, cannot speak or cry due to breathing difficulty, or is drooling and unable to swallow. Additionally, if stridor is getting louder or does not stop at rest, seek emergency care right away [S1].

question: My daughter touched a hot pan and burned her fingers a little. What's the first thing I should do?
reference_answer: Cool the burn immediately by running cool (not ice cold) water over it for 10–20 minutes, which is the single most important first aid step. Do not apply ice, butter, oil, or toothpaste.
source_excerpts:
[common-injuries-first-aid.pdf#1]
1. Burns in Children
Burns are classified by depth. Children have thinner skin than adults, so burns can be more severe and deeper than
they appear initially. Types of Burns
• First-degree burn (superficial): Affects only the outer layer of skin (epidermis). Red, dry, painful, no blisters. Like a mild sunburn. Heals in 3–5 days without scarring. • Second-degree burn (partial thickness): Affects the epidermis and part of the dermis. Red, blistered, very
painful, moist/weeping appearance. Heals in 2–3 weeks. May scar. Second-degree burns larger than 3 inches
or on the face, hands, feet, groin, or over a joint need medical attention. • Third-degree burn (full thickness): Destroys the full thickness of skin. May appear white, brown, or charred. May be painless because nerve endings are destroyed. Always requires emergency medical care. Skin grafting
may be needed. Common Causes in Children
• Scalds from hot liquids (most common in children under 5) — hot coffee, tea, soup, bathwater, steam
• Contact burns from touching hot surfaces — stoves, ovens, curling irons, space heaters, fireplaces
• Flame burns from fire, candles, lighters, matches
• Electrical burns from outlets, cords, appliances (always need medical evaluation even if skin looks fine)
• Chemical burns from cleaning products, drain cleaners, battery acid
• Sunburn from UV exposure
First Aid for Minor Burns (First-Degree and Small Second-Degree)
HOME CARE: Most minor burns can be treated at home. • Step 1 — Cool the burn immediately. Run cool (not ice cold) water over the burned area for 10–20 minutes. This is the single most important first aid step. Do this within the first few minutes for best results. • Step 2 — Remove clothing and jewelry from the burned area, unless stuck to the skin. If clothing is stuck,
do not pull it off — cut around it. • Step 3 — Protect the burn. After cooling, cover loosely with a clean, non-stick bandage or sterile gauze. Do
not wrap tightly. • Step 4 — Pain relief. Acetaminophen or ibuprofen (age-appropriate dosing) for pain. Cool compresses can
also help. • Step 5 — Moisturize. Once cooled, apply pure aloe vera gel or a gentle moisturizer. After the first 24 hours,
you can apply a thin layer of antibiotic ointment (like bacitracin) and re-cover with a non-stick bandage. Change
the bandage daily. • Step 6 — Watch for infection. Signs of infection: increasing redness, swelling, warmth, pus or cloudy
drainage, red streaks radiating from the burn, fever, or increasing pain after the first 24–48 hours.
answer: Cool the burn immediately by running cool (not ice cold) water over the burned area for 10–20 minutes. This is the single most important first aid step. After cooling, remove any clothing or jewelry from the burned area, unless it is stuck to the skin. If it is stuck, do not pull it off—cut around it. Protect the burn by covering it loosely with a clean, non-stick bandage or sterile gauze. Watch for signs of infection, such as increasing redness, swelling, warmth, pus, or fever [S1][S2]. If the burn is larger than 3 inches or on the face, hands, feet, groin, or over a joint, seek medical attention [S2].

6. Strep Throat
What Is Strep Throat
Strep throat is a bacterial infection of the throat and tonsils caused by Group A Streptococcus (GAS) bacteria. It
is most common in children ages 5 to 15 but can occur at any age. Strep throat is uncommon in children under
3 years. It spreads through respiratory droplets when an infected person coughs or sneezes, and through
shared food or drinks. Strep throat is different from a viral sore throat, which is more common and does not
require antibiotics. Symptoms
Strep throat symptoms usually appear 2 to 5 days after exposure and come on suddenly. • Severe sore throat that comes on quickly (not gradual like a cold)
• Pain and difficulty swallowing
• Fever, often 101 F or higher
• Red, swollen tonsils, sometimes with white patches or streaks of pus
• Tiny red spots (petechiae) on the roof of the mouth
• Swollen, tender lymph nodes in the front of the neck
• Headache, stomachache, nausea, or vomiting (especially in younger children)
• Body aches and general feeling of being unwell
• Sometimes a fine, red, sandpaper-like rash (scarlet fever)
Symptoms that suggest a viral sore throat rather than strep include: cough, runny nose, hoarseness,
conjunctivitis (pink eye), and diarrhea. Strep throat typically does NOT cause cough or runny nose. Diagnosis
Strep throat cannot be diagnosed by looking at the throat alone. A rapid strep test or throat culture is needed. The rapid test takes about 5 to 10 minutes. If the rapid test is negative but the doctor still suspects strep, a
throat culture may be sent to a lab (results in 1 to 2 days). Testing is important because strep requires antibiotic
treatment to prevent complications. Treatment
• Antibiotics are essential for strep throat. Penicillin or amoxicillin are the most commonly prescribed. For
penicillin-allergic patients, alternatives include azithromycin, cephalexin, or clindamycin
• The full course of antibiotics (usually 10 days) must be completed even if symptoms improve, to fully
eliminate the bacteria and prevent complications
• Children are no longer contagious after 12 to 24 hours of antibiotic treatment and can return to school or
daycare after at least 12 hours on antibiotics and no fever
• Pain and fever management: acetaminophen or ibuprofen
• Warm liquids like broth, warm water with honey (children over 1 year), or warm tea can soothe the throat
• Cold foods like popsicles and ice chips can also help with pain
• Gargling with warm salt water (older children who can gargle without swallowing)
• Rest and adequate hydration

typically last 10–20 minutes per side. • Signs the baby is getting enough: 6+ wet diapers per day by day 4, 3–4 stools per day in the first
month, steady weight gain, baby seems satisfied after feeding. • Growth spurts: Babies cluster feed (feed more frequently) during growth spurts, typically around 2–3
weeks, 6 weeks, 3 months, and 6 months. This is temporary and helps increase milk supply. Common Breastfeeding Challenges
• Sore nipples: Most common in the first week. Usually caused by a poor latch. Correct the latch, apply
expressed breast milk to nipples after feeding, allow them to air-dry. Lanolin cream can help. Persistent
pain beyond 1–2 weeks or cracked/bleeding nipples warrants evaluation. • Engorgement: Breasts become overly full, hard, and painful (usually days 3–5 when milk comes in). Feed frequently, apply warm compresses before feeding, cold compresses after, hand express a small
amount if needed to soften the breast for latch. • Mastitis: A breast infection causing localized redness, warmth, swelling, pain, and often fever/flu-like
symptoms. Continue breastfeeding (it will not harm the baby). Contact your doctor, as antibiotics may
be needed. • Low milk supply concerns: True low supply is rare. The best way to increase supply is to feed more
frequently and ensure good latch. Adequate hydration and nutrition for the mother are important. Pumping after feedings can also stimulate additional production. • Thrush: A yeast infection that can affect the baby's mouth (white patches on tongue, inner cheeks)
and the mother's nipples (pink, flaky, itchy, burning pain). Both mother and baby need treatment —
contact your pediatrician. Pumping and Storing Breast Milk
• Room temperature: Freshly expressed milk is safe for up to 4 hours at room temperature (up to 77°F
/ 25°C)
• Refrigerator: Up to 4 days at 40°F (4°C) or lower. Store in the back, not the door. • Freezer: Up to 6 months is optimal; up to 12 months is acceptable. Use freezer-safe breast milk
storage bags. • Thawing: Thaw in the refrigerator overnight, or hold under warm running water. Never microwave
breast milk (creates hot spots, destroys nutrients). Use thawed milk within 24 hours. Never refreeze
thawed milk. Source: AAP, HealthyChildren.org — Breastfeeding Basics; CDC Breast Milk Storage Guidelines

question: How long should my baby sleep in our bedroom, and is it okay to just have them sleep in our bed with us?
reference_answer: Room sharing (crib or bassinet in the parents' room within arm's reach) is recommended for at least the first 6 months, ideally the first year. Bed sharing is not recommended because it increases the risk of SIDS, suffocation, and entrapment.
source_excerpts:
[children-health-guide.pdf#7]
3. Sleep Safety and SIDS Prevention
Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS) is the unexplained death of a baby younger than 1 year, usually
occurring during sleep. While the exact cause is unknown, research has identified several evidence-based
practices that dramatically reduce the risk. The ABCs of Safe Sleep
A = Alone, B = Back, C = Crib — This is the foundation of safe infant sleep. Back to Sleep
• Always place babies on their BACK for every sleep — naps and nighttime. This single practice has
reduced SIDS deaths by over 50% since the 1990s. • Back sleeping is recommended until age 1, even after the baby can roll over on their own. Place them
on their back; if they roll to their stomach independently, you do not need to reposition them. • Side sleeping is NOT safe and is NOT recommended. Babies placed on their sides can easily roll onto
their stomachs. Safe Sleep Surface
• Use a firm, flat mattress in a safety-approved crib, bassinet, or play yard. The mattress should be
covered with only a fitted sheet. • Nothing else in the crib: No blankets, pillows, bumper pads, stuffed animals, positioners, wedges, or
loose bedding. These are suffocation and entrapment hazards. • The sleep surface should be flat (not inclined). Inclined sleepers, car seats, swings, and bouncers are
not safe for unsupervised sleep. • Do not use sleep positioners or nests (such as DockATot or Snuggle Me). These have not been
shown to be safe and the FDA has warned against them. Room Sharing (Not Bed Sharing)
• Room sharing is recommended for at least the first 6 months, ideally the first year. Place the crib or
bassinet in the parents' bedroom, within arm's reach. • Bed sharing is NOT recommended. Sharing a bed with an infant increases the risk of SIDS,
suffocation, and entrapment. This includes sharing with parents, siblings, or pets. • The risk of bed sharing is especially high if: a parent smokes, has consumed alcohol or sedating
medications, the baby is younger than 4 months, the baby was born preterm or with low birth weight, or
the sleep surface is soft (couch, armchair, waterbed). Additional SIDS Risk Reduction
• Offer a pacifier at sleep time: Pacifier use during sleep has been associated with reduced SIDS risk. If breastfeeding, wait until breastfeeding is well established (usually 3–4 weeks) before introducing a
pacifier. If it falls out during sleep, do not replace it. • Avoid overheating: Dress the baby in no more than one additional layer than what an adult would
wear. Watch for signs of overheating: sweating, damp hair, flushed cheeks, heat rash, rapid breathing.
answer: It is recommended that your baby sleep in your bedroom for at least the first 6 months, ideally for the first year. However, bed sharing is not recommended, as it increases the risk of Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS), suffocation, and entrapment. Instead, place the crib or bassinet in your bedroom within arm's reach [S1].

Ibuprofen is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) available over the counter. It reduces fever, relieves
pain, and reduces inflammation. Brand names include Motrin, Advil, and many generic brands. Unlike
acetaminophen, ibuprofen also has anti-inflammatory properties, making it particularly effective for pain

• Fever reduction
• Mild to moderate pain: headaches, toothaches, earaches, sore throat

• Inflammation: sprains, strains, minor injuries
• Menstrual cramps (older children and adolescents)

Do NOT give ibuprofen to infants younger than 6 months of age. I

• Do not give aspirin or other NSAIDs at the same time as ibuprofen

question: My toddler just had a seizure while running a high fever. What should I do while it's happening?
reference_answer: Place the child on their side on a safe surface, don't put anything in their mouth, don't restrain them, time the seizure, and call 911 if it lasts more than 5 minutes.
source_excerpts:
[pediatric-medical-reference.pdf#2]
• Acetaminophen (Tylenol) can be given every 4 to 6 hours as needed. Follow package directions based on
child's weight
• Ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin) can be given every 6 to 8 hours. Do not give ibuprofen to children younger than 6
months
• Never give aspirin to children or teenagers. Aspirin can cause Reye's syndrome, a rare but serious
condition
• Do not alternate between acetaminophen and ibuprofen unless directed by a healthcare provider, as this
can lead to dosing errors
Febrile Seizures
Some children experience seizures triggered by fever, called febrile seizures. These occur in about 2 to 5
percent of children between ages 6 months and 5 years. During a febrile seizure the child may shake, twitch,
stiffen, or become unresponsive for a short time, usually less than 5 minutes. While frightening, most febrile
seizures are harmless and do not cause lasting damage or epilepsy. If a seizure occurs: place the child on their
side on a safe surface, do not put anything in their mouth, do not restrain them, time the seizure, and call 911 if
it lasts more than 5 minutes. When to Call the Doctor
Any infant under 3 months with a rectal temperature of 100.4 F (38 C) or higher needs immediate medical
I
evaluation, even if no other symptoms are present
• Child 3 to 12 months with a fever of 102.2 F (39 C) or higher
• Child under 2 years with a fever lasting more than 48 hours
• Fever over 104 F (40 C) at any age
• Fever that keeps coming back over a week or more
• Child appears very ill, is unusually sleepy, or is very fussy
• Signs of dehydration: no wet diapers for 8 hours, no tears when crying, dry mouth, sunken eyes
• New rash accompanying the fever
• Stiff neck, severe headache, difficulty breathing, blue lips
• Child has a chronic medical condition or weakened immune system
Prevention
Frequent handwashing is the most effective way to prevent infections that cause fever. Keep children up to date
on immunizations. Teach children to cover coughs and sneezes. Avoid sharing cups and utensils. Keep
children home when they are sick to prevent spreading illness. Source: MedlinePlus/NIH, CDC Fever Guidelines, AAP HealthyChildren.org
answer: Call 911 right now. During a seizure, place your child on their side on a flat surface, do not put anything in their mouth, do not try to restrain them, and time the seizure. If the seizure lasts more than 5 minutes, call 911 again. After the seizure, monitor your child and seek medical attention as needed.
